meta.titre: Phillips Curve: the inflation and unemployment trade-off
meta.sous_theme: Short-run and long-run Phillips curves and expectations

sections.contenu_markdown: When a government announces a big programme of roads, schools and public works, many families hope for new jobs. Traders, however, soon worry that shops will raise their prices as more people have money to spend. The same policy that creates work may also push up the cost of living, and ministers must decide how much of each they can accept. The Phillips curve is the economist's picture of that dilemma. At A Level you must name it, describe the relationship it shows, and judge whether the trade-off lasts.

items: Inflation is a sustained rise in the general level of prices, measured as a percentage change in a price index.
The unemployment rate is the number of unemployed people as a percentage of the labour force.
A rise in aggregate demand tends to raise output and employment in the short run.

sections.titre: The Phillips curve: short-run trade-off and long-run limits
sections.contenu_markdown:
### The curve and its meaning
The **Phillips curve** shows the relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment. In 1958 A. W. Phillips reported, from data for the United Kingdom, an inverse relationship between unemployment and the rate of change of money wages. Later economists restated it with price inflation on the vertical axis and unemployment on the horizontal axis. The short-run curve slopes downwards, usually convex to the origin: low unemployment goes with high inflation, and high unemployment goes with low inflation.

### Why the trade-off arises
When aggregate demand rises, firms raise output and take on workers, so unemployment falls. Labour becomes scarce, workers bargain for higher wages, firms' costs rise and prices rise (cost-push), while strong spending also pulls prices up (demand-pull). The government therefore appears to face a choice between low inflation and low unemployment, two of its main objectives.

### Breakdown and the expectations-augmented curve
In the 1970s many economies suffered **stagflation**: high inflation and high unemployment together, often linked to rises in oil prices. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that workers bargain according to the inflation they **expect**. If the government pushes unemployment below the **natural rate of unemployment** (the rate at which the labour market is in balance and inflation is stable), inflation rises above what was expected. Once expectations adjust, the short-run curve shifts upwards and unemployment returns to the natural rate with higher inflation.

| | Short-run Phillips curve | Long-run Phillips curve |
|---|---|---|
| Shape | Downward sloping | Vertical at the natural rate |
| Trade-off | Yes, while expectations stay unchanged | No lasting trade-off |
| Shifts caused by | Changes in expected inflation, supply shocks | Supply-side changes that alter the natural rate |

### Policy implication
Demand-side policy can hold unemployment below the natural rate only temporarily, and at the price of rising inflation. To lower the natural rate itself, supply-side measures such as training, better job information and greater labour mobility are needed.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When a table of inflation and unemployment rates is given
variantes.contenu_markdown: Put the unemployment rate on the horizontal axis and the inflation rate on the vertical axis, label both with units, plot every pair of values, join the points with a smooth curve and give the graph a title. Name: Phillips curve. Relationship: inverse (negative), because when one variable rises the other falls. To measure the cost of lower unemployment, divide the rise in inflation by the fall in unemployment between two points.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question gives expected inflation and a natural rate
variantes.contenu_markdown: A simple model is $\pi = \pi^{e} + b\,(u_n - u)$, where $\pi$ is inflation, $\pi^{e}$ is expected inflation, $u_n$ is the natural rate, $u$ is actual unemployment and $b$ measures how strongly inflation responds. When $u = u_n$, actual inflation equals expected inflation. When $u$ is below $u_n$, inflation exceeds expectations; next period expectations rise and the whole short-run curve moves up.

variantes.nom: Evaluation: how useful is the curve?
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command is discuss, assess or to what extent
variantes.contenu_markdown: Useful: it makes the conflict between two objectives clear and helps policy makers see the short-run cost of reducing unemployment. Limited: the relationship is unstable, stagflation showed that supply shocks and expectations shift the curve, and there may be no lasting trade-off. Unemployment figures may also hide structural problems, for example where much work is informal, so measured unemployment may not reflect pressure in the labour market. Conclude that the curve is a good short-run guide but a poor long-run one.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The table gives hypothetical annual figures for an economy.

| Unemployment rate (%) | 3 | 4 | 5 | 7 | 9 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inflation rate (%) | 9 | 6 | 4 | 2.5 | 1.5 |

(a) Describe how to plot the data.
(b) Name the curve and state the relationship it shows.
(c) Calculate the rise in inflation per percentage point fall in unemployment between 5 and 3 per cent, and between 9 and 7 per cent.
(d) The government wants inflation below 5 per cent. Find the lowest unemployment rate it can reach in the table.

etapes.action: Choose the axes and plot the pairs.
etapes.justification: Convention puts the independent variable, unemployment, on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plot the points (3, 9), (4, 6), (5, 4), (7, 2.5) and (9, 1.5), join them with a smooth curve and label both axes in per cent.

etapes.action: Name the curve and read its direction.
etapes.justification: The points fall from left to right, so the variables move in opposite directions.
etapes.resultat_markdown: It is a **Phillips curve** and shows an **inverse (negative) relationship** between inflation and unemployment.

etapes.action: Measure the cost between 5 and 3 per cent.
etapes.justification: The cost of lower unemployment is the extra inflation divided by the fall in unemployment.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Inflation rises from 4 to 9, which is 5 points, for a fall of 2 points in unemployment: $5 \div 2 = 2.5$ points of inflation for each point of unemployment.

etapes.action: Measure the cost between 9 and 7 per cent.
etapes.justification: The same method is applied at the other end of the curve.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Inflation rises from 1.5 to 2.5, which is 1 point, for a fall of 2 points: $1 \div 2 = 0.5$ points of inflation for each point of unemployment.

etapes.justification: Only points with inflation below 5 per cent are acceptable.
etapes.resultat_markdown: At 4 per cent unemployment inflation is 6, which is too high; at 5 per cent it is 4, which is acceptable. The lowest unemployment rate available is **5 per cent**.

sections.conclusion_markdown: (a) Unemployment on the horizontal axis, inflation on the vertical axis, a smooth downward-sloping curve. (b) The Phillips curve; the relationship is inverse. (c) 2.5 points of extra inflation per point of unemployment at low unemployment, but only 0.5 at high unemployment, so the curve is steeper at low unemployment. (d) 5 per cent unemployment, with inflation at 4 per cent.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Phillips curve shows that when unemployment rises, inflation rises as well."
items.pourquoi_faux: The short-run curve slopes downwards: the relationship is inverse. High inflation and high unemployment together is a different case, called stagflation.
items.correction_markdown: The Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship: lower unemployment is associated with higher inflation, and higher unemployment with lower inflation.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Phillips curve shows the trade-off between inflation and the balance of payments."
items.pourquoi_faux: The curve involves two variables only, the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment (originally the change in wages).
items.correction_markdown: The Phillips curve shows the trade-off between inflation and unemployment, so it presents the government with a choice between price stability and full employment.

items.erreur_markdown: "The long-run Phillips curve slopes downwards, so a government can keep unemployment low for ever by accepting more inflation."
items.pourquoi_faux: Once workers expect the higher inflation, the short-run curve shifts up and unemployment returns to the natural rate.
items.correction_markdown: The long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment. Demand expansion gives only a temporary fall in unemployment and leaves permanently higher inflation.

items.erreur_markdown: "Stagflation proves that the Phillips curve was never valid."
items.pourquoi_faux: Stagflation showed that the short-run curve is unstable and shifts when supply shocks and expectations change. It did not show that a short-run trade-off cannot exist.
items.correction_markdown: Explain that the curve can shift upwards, so a given unemployment rate comes with higher inflation, while a short-run trade-off may still hold along each short-run curve.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) Name the curve that shows the relationship between inflation and unemployment.
(b) State the relationship it shows.
(c) Which two macroeconomic objectives does the government seem to choose between?
(d) What name is given to the situation in which inflation and unemployment are both high?
items.solution_markdown:
(a) The **Phillips curve**.
(b) An **inverse (negative) relationship**: as unemployment falls, inflation rises.
(c) **Price stability (low inflation) and full employment (low unemployment)**.
(d) **Stagflation**.

items.enonce_markdown:
An economy has the following hypothetical data.

| Unemployment rate (%) | 2 | 4 | 6 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Inflation rate (%) | 12 | 6 | 3 | 2 |

(a) Calculate the extra inflation per point of unemployment removed when unemployment falls from 6 to 4 per cent and from 4 to 2 per cent.
(b) What does the answer to (a) show about the shape of the curve?
(c) The government will accept inflation of at most 4 per cent. State the lowest unemployment rate it can aim for.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) 6 to 4: inflation rises from 3 to 6, so $3 \div 2 = 1.5$ points per point: **1.5**. 4 to 2: inflation rises from 6 to 12, so $6 \div 2 = 3$ points per point: **3**.
(b) The cost in extra inflation grows as unemployment falls, so the curve is steeper at low unemployment (convex to the origin).
(c) Inflation is 3 per cent at 6 per cent unemployment, within the limit, whereas at 4 per cent unemployment it is 6 per cent, which is too high: **6 per cent**.

items.enonce_markdown:
In a hypothetical economy, inflation follows $\pi = \pi^{e} + 2\,(6 - u)$ where $u$ is the unemployment rate in per cent and the natural rate is 6 per cent. In year 1 expected inflation is 3 per cent and the government holds unemployment at 4 per cent. In each later year, expected inflation equals the previous year's actual inflation.
(a) Calculate inflation in years 1, 2 and 3 if unemployment is kept at 4 per cent.
(b) In year 4, unemployment is allowed to rise to 7 per cent. Calculate inflation.
(c) Explain why the long-run Phillips curve is vertical.
(d) Suggest one policy that could lower the natural rate of unemployment.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Year 1: $3 + 2(6 - 4) = 7$. Year 2: expected inflation is 7, so $7 + 4 = 11$. Year 3: expected inflation is 11, so $11 + 4 = 15$. The answers are **7, 11 and 15 per cent**: inflation accelerates.
(b) Expected inflation is 15, so $15 + 2(6 - 7) = 13$: inflation is **13 per cent**. It falls only slowly, which shows the cost of bringing down inflation that has become expected.
(c) In the long run expectations adjust fully, so actual inflation equals expected inflation and unemployment settles at the natural rate whatever the level of inflation. Every steady inflation rate therefore goes with the same unemployment rate, there is no lasting trade-off, and the curve is a vertical line at the natural rate.
(d) A supply-side measure, for example **training programmes** or **better information on job vacancies**, which reduces structural and frictional unemployment.

items_markdown: The Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment, so the government seems to face a choice between price stability and full employment.
The trade-off arises because falling unemployment raises wage pressure and demand pressure on prices.
To answer data questions, plot unemployment horizontally and inflation vertically, join the points smoothly, name the curve and describe the inverse relationship.
Stagflation and workers' expectations showed that the short-run curve shifts. The long-run curve is vertical at the natural rate of unemployment.
Demand policy gives only a temporary fall in unemployment below the natural rate; supply-side policy is needed to lower the natural rate.
